title: What training must NSW out-of-home care agencies give carers and staff?
description: NSW out-of-home care training: the Code of Practice in force since October 2025, pre-authorization carer training, annual reviews and Child Safe Standard 7.
shortAnswer: Designated agencies providing statutory out-of-home care in New South Wales must meet both the 10 Child Safe Standards and the Office of the Children's Guardian Code of Practice, the accreditation criteria since October 1, 2025. The Code requires training for prospective carers before authorization and for staff when they start, an annual review of each caregiver's training needs, planned ongoing training, and child protection training that covers protective behaviors and responding to disclosures.
keyTakeaways: The Code of Practice for designated agencies and adoption service providers commenced on October 1, 2025, replacing the 23 Child Safe Standards for Permanent Care, and the Children's Guardian Regulation 2022 was amended to reflect it.

Prospective carers must receive relevant training before authorization, and the agency must record on the Carers Register that pre-authorization training is complete and the Code of Conduct for Authorised Carers has been read and signed.

Agencies must review caregivers' training and support needs at least annually and give everyone who works with children training on child protection, protective behaviors and responding to disclosures.
Residential care workers must be entered on the Residential Care Workers Register, in operation since July 18, 2022, before they provide care.
The Office of the Children's Guardian can issue compliance notices or accept enforceable undertakings under the Child Safe Scheme, and fines can follow non-compliance with either.
regulator: Office of the Children's Guardian (NSW), which accredits designated agencies and regulates the Child Safe Scheme
appliesTo: Designated agencies accredited to provide statutory or supported out-of-home care in NSW (foster, relative and kinship care, and residential care)
Principal Officers and governing bodies of accredited agencies
Authorised carers, prospective carers and residential care workers
Caseworkers and other staff who work with children in care

sections.heading: Which rules set training duties for NSW out-of-home care agencies?

blocks.text: Two overlapping instruments, both regulated by the Office of the Children's Guardian (OCG). First, the Child Safe Scheme under the Children's Guardian Act 2019 requires designated agencies and adoption service providers to implement the 10 Child Safe Standards ([who the Standards apply to](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/child-safe-scheme/implementing-child-safe-standards/who-child-safe-standards-apply)). Second, the Code of Practice for Designated Agencies and Adoption Service Providers is the accreditation criteria against which agencies are assessed. This page states the position as at November 2026.

The OCG states that the Code of Practice commenced on October 1, 2025, replacing the 23 Child Safe Standards for Permanent Care, and that the Children's Guardian Regulation 2022 was amended on the same date to reflect it ([information for accredited agencies](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/organisations/statutory-out-home-care-and-adoption/information-accredited-agencies)). The OCG's [Code of Practice Implementation Handbook](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-03/g-soohc_codeimplementation.pdf) (March 2025) reproduces the practice requirements and explains how assessors test them. The clause numbers on this page follow that handbook.

Other sectors under the Child Safe Scheme have their own pages. For early childhood services in NSW, see [child protection training for NSW early childhood services](/regulations/child-protection-training-early-childhood-nsw); for screening, see [Working with Children Check requirements](/regulations/working-with-children-check-requirements).

sections.heading: What does the Code of Practice require for carer and staff training?

blocks.text: Clause 31 (Support and training), under practice requirement 5 that persons who work with and care for children are suitable and supported, sets the training cycle for both caregivers and staff. As reproduced in the OCG handbook, an entity must:

items: provide relevant training to prospective carers, prospective guardians and prospective adoptive parents **before** their authorization or approval;
provide relevant training to a staff member at the commencement of their engagement;
give everyone who works with and cares for children regular supervision and support, and opportunities to raise concerns and seek additional support and training;
review the training and support needs of caregivers **at least annually**;
have processes for reviewing staff performance and identifying training and support needs;
provide ongoing training opportunities and have a planned approach to ongoing education and training; and
give carers information about other carer support services and advocacy organizations.

blocks.text: Clause 19 adds a governance duty: an entity must ensure staff who work with and care for children have the training, supervision, support and resources necessary to perform their roles. The handbook says assessors ask how the governing body knows that staff and caregivers are receiving the support, supervision and training they need, so training data has to reach the board, not stay with the learning team.

sections.heading: What child protection training must carers and staff receive?

blocks.text: Clause 32 (Training and procedures), under practice requirement 6 on child protection and child safety, requires an entity to give every person who works with and cares for children three things: information about their responsibility to report concerns about risks to child safety; training on child protection and child safety, including how to talk to children about protective behaviors; and training on how to respond to disclosures of harm made by a child.

The same clause requires clear information about roles, responsibilities and expectations for behavior toward children, policies to identify, report, manage and review all incidents affecting a child, and reporting of risk of significant harm under Chapter 3, Part 2 of the Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998. The training is therefore assessable against concrete agency procedures, not just general awareness.

These duties sit on top of Child Safe Standard 7, which the OCG words as "Staff are equipped with the knowledge, skills and awareness to keep children safe through continual education and training", with elements covering indicators of maltreatment (particularly organizational child abuse), the organization's child safe practices, and practical skills in responding to disclosures ([what are the Child Safe Standards](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/child-safe-scheme/what-are-child-safe-standards)). In out-of-home care, the Code makes that standard specific: it names carers as well as staff, and adds protective behaviors. For reporting duties generally, see [mandatory reporting training in Australia](/regulations/mandatory-reporting-training-australia).

sections.heading: What must happen before a foster, relative or kinship carer is authorized?

blocks.text: Pre-authorization training is one of several gates recorded on the Carers Register. The handbook states that before authorizing a carer, the designated agency must register the person and household members on the Carers Register and complete mandatory checks: identification, Working with Children Check, National Police Check, Community Services Check, other designated agency check, health check and a minimum of 2 reference checks.

The agency must also ensure that the Code of Conduct for Authorised Carers has been sighted and signed, that pre-authorization training has been completed, and that carer capability and suitability, including household members, has been assessed. The Code of Conduct for Authorised Carers is issued by the Minister under section 248C of the Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998, and the handbook notes that failing to comply with it may lead to the carer's authorization being cancelled or suspended.

The Carers Register acts as a licensing tool, issuing a carer authorization number that is needed before the person can provide care, and it lets agencies see the application and authorization history of anyone who applies to them ([foster carers](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/parents-and-carers/foster-carers)). Each Principal Officer, who authorizes carers, must hold a Working with Children Check clearance verified by the agency.

sections.heading: What applies to residential care workers?

blocks.text: Residential care workers must be on the Residential Care Workers Register before they provide care in a residential setting. The OCG states the register commenced on July 18, 2022 and responds to a Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse recommendation for carer registers ([Residential Care Workers Register](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/organisations/statutory-out-home-care-and-adoption/residential-care-worker-register)). The handbook lists the mandatory probity checks as a National Police Check, other designated agency check and Working with Children Check, with a Community Services Check to commence at a later date.

Clause 31(2) means each residential care worker must receive relevant training at the start of their engagement, and clause 32 applies to them as people who work with and care for children. Because residential settings include temporary accommodation such as hotels and serviced apartments, agencies should make sure induction reaches staff placed there, including workers referred by labor hire agencies, who the handbook says are also recorded on the register.

sections.heading: How does the Office of the Children's Guardian monitor and enforce these duties?

blocks.text: Through accreditation monitoring and the Child Safe Scheme's enforcement powers. Under its monitoring and assessment framework, the OCG has more regular contact with agencies during the accreditation cycle through Agency Status Updates, scheduled assessment and risk based responsive monitoring. Under the Child Safe Scheme it may request a child safe recruitment, induction and training policy, inspect premises, direct a Child Safe Self-Assessment, issue a compliance notice or accept an enforceable undertaking, and fines can follow if either is not followed ([monitoring and enforcement](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/child-safe-scheme/implementing-child-safe-standards/monitoring-and-enforcement)).

On October 16, 2026 the Children's Guardian released a new regulatory framework that brings the OCG's schemes, including the Child Safe Scheme, the Working with Children Check, the NDIS Worker Check, the Reportable Conduct Scheme and out-of-home care regulation, into one risk based, prevention focused approach ([new regulatory framework](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/news/new-regulatory-framework-strengthens-child-safety-across-nsw)). Agencies that also deliver disability supports should align this work with [NDIS worker screening](/regulations/ndis-worker-screening-requirements). A public sector view is on the [government sector page](/industries/government-defence).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry can model each Code of Practice clause as an obligation with defined learning outcomes for carers and for staff, so pre-authorization training, induction and the annual caregiver review all trace to the clause they satisfy. That supports the evidence OCG assessors request and shows the governing body where training gaps sit.

faqs.q: Does the NSW Code of Practice set a minimum number of training hours for foster carers?
faqs.a: No. The Code requires relevant training before authorization, an annual review of each caregiver's training and support needs, ongoing training opportunities and a planned approach, but it does not set hours or a named course. The OCG handbook says agencies are best placed to decide what evidence demonstrates compliance.

faqs.q: Did the Code of Practice replace the Child Safe Standards for out-of-home care?
faqs.a: It replaced the 23 Child Safe Standards for Permanent Care as accreditation criteria from October 1, 2025. Designated agencies must still implement the 10 Child Safe Standards under the Child Safe Scheme, because they are listed among the entities required to apply them.

faqs.q: Can a Principal Officer delegate carer authorization?
faqs.a: Yes, with approval from the Children's Guardian. The Principal Officer must make a written request explaining why, identifying the proposed delegate and their suitability, confirming the delegate holds a Working with Children Check clearance or application verified by the agency, and stating how long the delegation will last.

faqs.q: Do residential care workers need pre-authorization training like foster carers?
faqs.a: Clause 31(1) names prospective carers, guardians and adoptive parents for pre-authorization training. Residential care workers are staff, so clause 31(2) requires relevant training at the start of their engagement, and clause 32 requires child protection, protective behaviors and disclosure training for them too.

Code clause 32 Training and procedures: information on reporting responsibilities, training on child protection and child safety including protective behaviours, training on responding to disclosures.
